text.p: Portuguese cement group Cimpor-Cimentos de Portugal should post net profit before all extraordinaries of 18.5-21.8 billion escudos for 1996, up from 17 billion the previous year, analysts said.
But there were doubts about whether the company would pay an extra high dividend, as some had hoped, financed by proceeds from the sale of its holding in Banco de Fomento & Exterior.
Cimpor's profit for 1995 rose to 18 billion when a roughly one billion escudo book profit from its holding in BFE is included. It posts its results on Wednesday.
The 1996 results are net of the 10.7 billion profit that the company earned from the sale of its BFE stake last year.
Analysts will be particularly keen to see the trend of the market in Spain and the state of play at its Alhandra plant were production was stopped at one time.

They said that concern over what was happening at Alhandra, its largest plant, was one factor depressing the price in recent weeks, with the share easing to 3,495 escudos from a late January high of 3,865 escudos.
"At the moment, the biggest question is the stoppage at Alhandra, which could be reflected in the results," said one analyst.
But Isabel Falkenberg of Finantia said that any difficulty at Alhandra, even if it is the company's biggest facility, could be compensated for with greater output from other plants.

The company has not said whether the stoppage at Alhandra affected just one oven nor is it known the exact period of the downtime. The work was intended to boost capacity from some 2.2 million tonnes a year. Cimpor's total output is some 7.4 million.
Analysts noted that while consumption grew in Portugal last year, it fell in Spain, a major market.
"Taking into account that Spain represents around 21 percent (of Cimpor sales) and if, suddenly, this market fell, it would have an immediate impact on sales," said Falkenberg.
Neverthless, analysts said that profits should still be pretty good.
"For 1996, I am looking for 18.67 billion escudos and a 15 percent gain to 32.3 billion before tax and extraordinaries," said James Harrison of Midas.
"The (share price) correction is explained by less aggressive forecasts for profit than, for example, in January and also by declining optimism about an extra dividend," said another analyst.
"The level of the dividend is a question mark...it is not known whether it will contain an extraordinary component for the book profit on BFE," the analyst added.
Cimpor paid out a gross dividend of 115 escudos on its 1995 results and has declared its intention to pay out at least 50 percent of net profit, excluding extraordinary gains.
"With the purchases in Brazil, it will be more difficult to pay out an extraordinary dividend," said Falkenberg.
Harrison said he was looking for a dividend of 125 escudos, adding that he thought the probability of a special dividend payout was less than 50 percent.
